Sanskrit-College-Library-Manuscript
                    Ātmabodhaṭīkā
                    Written in clear Bengali script on machine-made paper. It contains 17
                                folia (34 pages) of 10.75" x 4" size, each page containing 6 lines.
                                It contains only the commentary entitled Ātmabodhaṭīkā without the
                                text of Ātmabodha. No name of the author or the scribe is mentioned
                                anywhere. It is full of misreadings and omissions.

India-Office-Library-Manuscript
                    Ātmabodhaprakaraṇaṃ saṭīkam
                    This is microfilm copy of the manuscript deposited in the India
                                Office Library, London. The manuscript its numbered as--Sanskrit
                                2296. Egg 2296, I.O. 2011a, and bears the title Ātmabodhaprakaraṇaṃ
                                saṭīkam. It contains both the text and the commentary of the
                                Ātmabodha. It is complete in 16 folia with 10 to 12 lines on each
                                page. It is written in Devanāgarī script without any mention of
                                date, author or scribe. But a colophon with Śaṅkarācārya's name as
                                the author of the Ātmabodha appears at the end.

children.translated_text: <s>Ātmabodha</s> (Self-Knowledge)
For those whose sins have been destroyed by austerities, who are tranquil, free from passion,
this <s>Ātmabodha</s> (Self-Knowledge) is set forth for the benefit of those who seek liberation. ||1||
<s>Ātmabodhaṭīkā</s> (Commentary on the Ātmabodha)
Oṃ, salutations to <s>Durgā</s>.
the blessed <s>Śaṃkarācārya</s>, having composed the <s>Vedāntaprasthānatraya</s> (three foundational texts of Vedānta) for the most qualified students,

children.translated_text: wishing to show this treatise called <s>Ātmabodha</s>, which is a compendium of <s>Vedānta</s> conclusions, for the benefit of those of dull intellect who are unable to study those [three texts],
makes a declaration—[beginning with the words] 'tapobhiḥ' ('by austerities').
Here,

children.text:
nuṣṭhānarūpaistapobhiḥ
                        kṣīṇāni pāpāni rāgādyantaḥkaraṇadoṣā yeṣāṃ teṣāṃ, nityanaimittikaireva
                        kurvāṇo duritakṣayamiti vacanāt
children.translated_text: by such austerities, those whose sins—namely, the defects of the inner organ such as attachment and the like—have been destroyed; as stated in the scriptural declaration, 'By performing the regular and occasional rites alone, one accomplishes the destruction of sin.'

children.text:
This portion of the verse

children.translated_text: By austerities in the form of the performance of <s>Kṛcchra</s>, <s>Cāndrāyaṇa</s>, and regular (<s>nitya</s>) and occasional (<s>naimittika</s>) rites—
for those seekers of liberation who have made extensive effort toward breaking the knot of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly bondage),
who are endowed with the qualifications described—this <s>Ātmabodha</s> is set forth, meaning it is taught as mandatory through the form of an injunction. ||1||
Therefore, for those who are tranquil, whose minds are undisturbed, who are free from passion, devoid of desire for the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter—
Knowledge alone is the direct and sole means to liberation, superior to all other means;

children.text: pākasya vahnivajjñānaṃ vinā mokṣo na sidhyati ||2||
children.translated_text: just as cooking [cannot be accomplished] without fire, liberation is not accomplished without knowledge. ||2||

children.text:
nanu tapoyogamantrakarmayāgādyanekasādhaneṣu satsu mokṣaṃ prati bodha eva
                        kimiti prādhānyena ucyate ityata

children.translated_text: he says—[beginning with] 'bodho'nya' ('knowledge, compared to other [means]').
Now, when there exist many means such as austerity, yoga, mantras, ritual actions, sacrifices, and so forth, why is knowledge alone spoken of as primary for liberation? To this,
these means, through a sequence of successive steps,

children.text:
jñānadvārā
                        mokṣaṃ sādhayanti, jñānantu svajanmamātrādevājñānaṃ niḥśeṣaṃ nāśayitvā
                        mumukṣuṃ svārājye'bhiṣecayati, ato'nyasādhanebhyo jñānasya prādhānyamuktam
                        |
children.translated_text: accomplish liberation through knowledge; but knowledge, merely by its own arising, completely destroys ignorance and enthrones the seeker of liberation in his own sovereignty. Therefore, the primacy of knowledge over other means is stated.
Austerity, yoga, mantras, ritual actions, sacrifices, and the like—
[beginning with] 'pākasya' ('of cooking').
He confirms this with an example—
even when there are means such as firewood, water, vessels, and so forth, without fire,

children.text:
sidhyati tadvat
                        jñānaṃ vinā mokṣo na sidhyatītyartha ||2||
children.translated_text: is not accomplished—similarly, without knowledge, liberation is not accomplished. This is the meaning. ||2||
Just as in the world, the act of cooking,
Action, being non-opposed [to ignorance], cannot remove ignorance;
knowledge alone destroys ignorance, just as light destroys a mass of darkness. ||3||
Anticipating this doubt, he says—

children.text:
tyāśaṃkya
                                karmājñānayorvirodhābhāvānnaivamityāha--avirodhīti |
                                karmaṇo'vidyāvirodhitvābhāvādajñānaṃ nāśayituṃ notsahate vidyāyāḥ
                                prakāśarūpatvādaṃdhaṃ tamastejapuñjamiva nāśayituṃ samartha
                                ityarthaḥ

children.translated_text: [beginning with] 'avirodhitayā'—the meaning is clear. ||3||
Now, since actions possess diverse powers, could not action itself destroy ignorance?
as if by ignorance, upon the destruction of that [ignorance], it stands alone;
[Though the Self appears] limited
the <s>Ātman</s> (Self) indeed shines by itself, like the sun when the clouds have passed. ||4||
it were [finite]; how then can absolute aloneness (<s>kaivalya</s>)
[be attained]? To this he says—[beginning with] 'paricchinna' ('limited').
Now, the <s>Ātman</s> appears limited in each body as if

children.text:
which is
                            evidently a misreading. IM reads

ātmā kevala eva prakāśate
                        meghāvaraṇābhāve bhānuvadityarthaḥ ||4||
children.translated_text: the <s>Ātman</s> shines as absolute alone, like the sun in the absence of cloud cover. This is the meaning. ||4||

The limitedness of the <s>Ātman</s>, which is complete and without a second, is merely due to the superimposition of various high and low bodies imagined by ignorance, not from the standpoint of reality. Therefore, through discrimination, when non-discrimination is removed,
The <s>jīva</s> (individual soul), tainted by ignorance, [is made] completely pure through the practice of knowledge;
having purified [it], knowledge itself perishes, like the <s>kataka</s> nut [powder] in water. ||5||
the establishment of non-duality is improper [if it involves a] mental modification (<s>vṛtti</s>)—
since by [such] knowledge duality would be established. To this he says—[beginning with] 'ajñānakaluṣam' ('tainted by ignorance').
Now, from Self-knowledge,
made impure, identifying with agency, enjoyership, and so forth—
such a <s>jīva</s>—knowledge,
through prolonged practice, by means of the removal of ignorance, completely [destroys] its effects such as the inner organ and the rest,
and having destroyed [them], itself also
perishes, because the mental modification is an effect of ignorance. That
reflected knowledge, being a semblance of the <s>Ātman</s>, merges into the <s>Ātman</s> itself;

children.text:
ekībhavati; tadānīmadvaya evātmā prakāśate,
                        yathā katakareṇurakhilaṃ jalaṃ nirmalaṃ kṛtvā svayamapi
children.translated_text: it becomes one [with it]. At that time, the non-dual <s>Ātman</s> alone shines forth, just as the <s>kataka</s> nut, having made all the water pure, itself also
perishes—similarly is the meaning. ||5||
By ego-sense and the like, which are effects of ignorance,
<s>Saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence) is indeed like a dream, filled with attachment, aversion, and the like;
it appears as if real during its own time, but upon awakening, it ceases to be real. ||6||

children.text:
nanvaparokṣatayānubhūyamānasya saṃsārasya kathamatyantāsattvaṃ
                        pratyakṣavirūddhamityāśaṃkya svapnadṛṣṭāntena tasya

children.translated_text: he establishes its falsity—[beginning with] 'saṃsāra.'

Now, anticipating the doubt: 'How can the absolute non-existence of <s>saṃsāra</s>, which is experienced as immediately present, [be maintained]—is this not contradicted by direct perception?'—using the example of a dream,
being filled [with them], during its own time—

children.text:
svasya kāraṇabhūtājñāne sthite sati
                        tāvanmithyābhūto'pi saṃsāraḥ sannevāvabhāti
children.translated_text: that is, so long as the ignorance which is its cause persists, <s>saṃsāra</s>, though false, appears as if real;
but upon awakening, that is, upon the meaning of the [Vedāntic] statement—
through hearing [the scripture], when Self-knowledge arises, [saṃsāra] becomes entirely non-existent,
it ceases to be.
<s>Saṃsāra</s>, with attachment, aversion, and the like,
the example is: 'like a dream.'
Here,

children.text:
yāvannidrānubhūyate tāvanmithyābhūto'pi
                        satya iva bhāti, prabodhe nidrānāśe sati svapno mithyā bhavati, tadvat
                        saṃsāra ityarthaḥ
children.translated_text: so long as sleep is experienced, though false, appears as if real; upon awakening, when sleep is destroyed, the dream becomes [recognized as] false—similarly with <s>saṃsāra</s>. This is the meaning.
A dream also,
The world appears as real only so long [as Brahman is not known], just as silver [appears] in a shell;
until <s>Brahman</s>, the substratum of all, the non-dual, is known. ||7||
he confirms with an example—[beginning with] 'tāvat.'
The falsity of the world—

children.text:
tathā sarvādhiṣṭḥānabhūtaṃ
                        saccidānandādvayaṃ brahma yāvanna jñāyate sākṣānnānubhūyate
children.translated_text: similarly, so long as <s>Brahman</s>, which is the substratum of all, of the nature of <s>saccidānanda</s> (existence-consciousness-bliss) and non-dual, is not directly known and experienced,
until then, <s>saṃsāra</s>, appearing in the form of the world, [seems] real—
it is seen through delusion [as if real]. This is the meaning. ||7||
Just as, so long as the specific knowledge of the blue-backed, triangular, and other [characteristics of the shell] does not arise, the cognition of silver is experienced as if real—
In <s>Parameśvara</s> (the Supreme Lord), who is the material cause and the support of all, the worlds

devatiryaṅnarasthāvarajaṅgamādayo'pi

children.translated_text: In that which is of the nature of truth, knowledge, and bliss, eternal, pervading all—
Like space, <s>Hṛṣīkeśa</s> (the Lord of the senses), the all-pervading one, associated with various limiting adjuncts,
appears as if different due to their differences; upon the destruction of those [adjuncts], He becomes absolute. ||10||
He confirms the stated meaning with the example of space—[beginning with] 'yathākāśaḥ.'

children.text:
niyāmako vā,
                            vibhuḥ sarvagataḥ parameśvaraḥ svamāyākalpita
children.translated_text: or the controller; the all-pervading, omnipresent <s>Parameśvara</s>, through His own <s>Māyā</s>-projected
various kinds of limiting adjuncts, being reflected [therein], appears as manifold;

children.text:
, tannāśe sati brahmātmaikyajñānena
                            taṣāṃ māyāparikalpitānāṃ nāśāt
children.translated_text: upon the destruction of those, through the knowledge of the identity of <s>Brahman</s> and <s>Ātman</s>, since those <s>Māyā</s>-projected [adjuncts] are destroyed,

children.text:
kevala eva
                            bhāti, yathākāśo ?bopādhivaśānnāneva bhāti upādhilayādeka
children.translated_text: He shines as absolute alone, just as space, due to [pot and other] limiting adjuncts, appears as many, but upon the dissolution of the adjuncts, becomes one
alone—similarly is the meaning. ||10||
<s>Hṛṣīkeśa</s>—the impeller of all senses beginning with the mind,
Due to various limiting adjuncts alone, caste, name, stage of life, and the like
are superimposed on the <s>Ātman</s>, like differences of taste and color in water. ||11||
how can eternality be stated of that which is pervaded by the respective castes and so forth? To this he says—[beginning with] 'nānopādhi.'
Now, in all bodies,
superimposed on the <s>Ātman</s>, projected by <s>Māyā</s>, not inherently [belonging to it];

children.text:
, yathā svabhāvamadhuraṃ jalaṃ
                        kaṭukaṣāyāmlaraktapītādidravyopetaṃ sat tadrupaṃ bhajati
children.translated_text: just as water, which is by nature sweet, when combined with bitter, astringent, sour, red, yellow, and other substances, takes on their appearance,
but not in its own nature—
similarly is the meaning. ||11||
Due to the previously mentioned various limiting adjuncts alone, caste, name, stage of life, and the like are
Born from the five great elements that have undergone quintuplication (<s>pañcīkaraṇa</s>), fashioned by <s>karma</s>—
the [gross] body is said to be the locus of experience of pleasure and pain. ||12||
he describes—[beginning with] 'pañcīkṛta.'
The three limiting adjuncts of the <s>Ātman</s>, imagined by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance)—
dividing each into two halves,

children.text:
tatraikaikamardhaṃ caturdhā samaṃ
                        vibhacya svāṃśaṃ parityacyetareṣu yojanaṃ pañcīkaraṇam; evaṃ pañcīkṛtebhyaḥ
                        sthūlapṛthivyādimahābhūtebhyaḥ sambhavo yasya tat karmasaṃcitaṃ
children.translated_text: then dividing each half into four equal parts and combining [each half with a quarter of each of the other four]—this is <s>pañcīkaraṇa</s> (quintuplication). That which has its origin from the gross great elements such as earth and the rest that have undergone such quintuplication, and which is fashioned by <s>karma</s>—
constructed by <s>prārabdha karma</s> (karma that has begun to bear fruit), this gross body is the locus of the experiences of pleasure and pain,
the place of experience for the inner <s>Ātman</s>. ||12||
Of the five elements,
Endowed with the five <s>prāṇas</s> (vital breaths), mind, intellect, and the ten senses—
born from the elements that have not undergone quintuplication, the subtle body is the instrument of experience. ||13||
He describes the subtle limiting adjunct—[beginning with] 'pañcaprāṇa.'

children.text:
pañcaprāṇā ekasyaiva mahāprāṇasya prāṇādayo vṛttayaḥ,
                        jñānendriyakarmendriyabhedenendriyāṇi daśa, manaḥśabdena
                            saṃkalpavikalpātmakāntaḥkaraṇavṛtti

buddhirniścayātmikā,
                        etaiḥ saṃyuktamapañcīkṛtasūkṣmabhūtoththaṃ sūkṣmabhūtebhyo jātaṃ sūkṣmāṅgaṃ
                        liṅgaśarīraṃ sukhaduḥkhabhogasādhanamityarthaḥ
children.translated_text: intellect is that which has the nature of determination. Endowed with these, born from the subtle elements that have not undergone quintuplication—the subtle body, the <s>liṅga-śarīra</s>, is the instrument for the experience of pleasure and pain. This is the meaning.

The five <s>prāṇas</s> are the modifications such as <s>prāṇa</s> and the rest of the one great vital breath; the ten senses are divided into the cognitive senses and the active senses; by the word 'mind' is meant the function of the inner organ characterized by deliberation and conceptualization—
Beginningless <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), which is indescribable, is called the causal limiting adjunct;
one should ascertain the <s>Ātman</s> as different from the three limiting adjuncts. ||14||
He describes the third, the causal limiting adjunct—[beginning with] 'anādyavidyā.'

children.text:
kāraṇopādhirūcyate,
                        sā ca vyaṣṭisamaṣṭibhedena sthūlasūkṣmaprapañcayoḥ kāraṇabhūtatvāt
                        kāraṇopādhirūcyate |
children.translated_text: it is called the causal limiting adjunct. And it is called the causal adjunct because, in its individual (<s>vyaṣṭi</s>) and collective (<s>samaṣṭi</s>) aspects, it is the cause of both the gross and subtle phenomenal world.
Indescribable as either real or unreal, beginningless—
He states the purpose of describing the three adjuncts—[beginning with] 'upādhitritayāt anyam.'
One should ascertain the <s>Ātman</s> as the witness of those [three adjuncts]—one should know [it]. This is the meaning. ||14||
Through association with the five sheaths and the like, [the Self] appears as if made of each of them;
the pure <s>Ātman</s>, like a crystal [appearing colored] through association with blue cloth and the like. ||15||

dīnāṃ grahaṇam, etauryogena

not actually colored by them, even though [appearing] as if tinged.

The <s>annamaya</s> (food), <s>prāṇamaya</s> (vital breath), <s>manomaya</s> (mind), <s>vijñānamaya</s> (intellect), and <s>ānandamaya</s> (bliss) are the five sheaths. By the word 'ādi' (and the like), hunger

children.translated_text: The [Upaniṣadic passage] '<s>sa vā eṣa puruṣo'nnarasamayaḥ</s>' (This person indeed consists of the essence of food) and so forth indicates <s>Brahman</s> as situated in limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhis</s>) only for the purpose of revealing the subtle reality, not from the standpoint of ultimate truth — just as a pure crystal, through conjunction with blue, yellow cloth and such, appears as though it were made of each of those,
in reality there is no coloring — likewise [for <s>Brahman</s>] — this is the meaning. [15]
The body, endowed with sheaths (<s>kośas</s>) like husks and such, through the sifting by reasoning —
one should discriminate the inner, pure <s>ātman</s> (self), just as [one extracts] the rice grain. [16]
He states the method of discriminating the knowledge of the unattached nature of the self — [with the verse beginning] '<s>vapus</s>' (body):

Distinct from the body, senses, mind, intellect, and <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature),
